title: The Different Dynamics of Teaching Lower Set Classes
author: Dr Dario Emanuele
summary: A short practitioner's note arguing that the standard repertoire of participation routines does not simply scale down to a small lower-set class. Emanuele's claim is not that the strategies stop working but that they need rethinking, and he sorts them into what degrades and what improves at small group size. Turn and talk goes flat when pairs run out of things to say, choral response with eight or ten voices is weak and awkward rather than unifying, and think-pair-share stretches out painfully where confidence and vocabulary are thin. In their place he proposes whole-group individual response, keyword practice taken student by student, and one-to-one micro-interventions that are only affordable when the class is small. The piece closes with a morale argument aimed at teachers who feel demoralised by a lower-set allocation: the smaller group buys knowledge of each student, room to adapt in the moment, and visible small wins. It is a useful corrective to the assumption that a technique validated in a class of twenty-five transfers unchanged to a class of eight.
points: The organising insight is that participation routines depend on volume and social cover - remove twenty voices and choral response or turn and talk lose the energy and anonymity that made them safe.
Emanuele's substitution is accountability-based: every student answers or says the keyword in turn, which both raises accountability and gives the teacher a cleaner check on understanding.
One-to-one micro-interventions are framed as the small class's actual comparative advantage, because sitting beside a student to unpack a misconception is simply unaffordable in a large group.
Think-pair-share is singled out as the worst offender in a small group, where it risks silence or off-task chat instead of exchange.
The closing mindset argument treats a lower set as an opportunity for knowing students individually rather than a punishment, and ties that reframe to the teacher's own working life.
quotes: Teaching a smaller, lower set class feels very different from standing in front of an average-sized group. Many of the strategies that usually work wonders in a larger class lose their edge when you shrink the numbers. That doesn’t mean they stop working altogether — just that they need rethinking.

In a larger class, this creates a buzz of conversation and gives lots of students a safe way to rehearse their thinking. In a small group, it can feel flat — especially if students are reluctant or if pairs quickly run out of things to say.
With 25 voices, this creates energy and a sense of unity. With 8 or 10 voices, the effect is weak, sometimes even awkward, and students are more likely to hold back.

Instead of a paired conversation, ask each student to repeat an explanation or share their thinking. Everyone hears the key idea multiple times, you check the quality of answers, and you can reinforce keywords.

Small classes mean you can afford the time to sit beside a student, unpack a misconception, or give personal feedback. These micro-interventions can be transformative, and they’re only really possible with smaller groups.

Sometimes, the key is to shift our mindset: instead of wishing for a bigger, higher set group, lean into the unique advantages of a smaller class. It won’t solve every challenge — but it can make our teaching (and our working life) a lot happier.
